originalGroup.material:
My first climbing lesson

Saturday, 8 February

Today I went to an indoor climbing centre with our youth group. A qualified instructor checked our equipment and explained the activity before we approached the wall. ____1____ I had expected to start climbing immediately, but the preparation was part of the lesson.

On my first attempt, I reached a blue hold and stopped. The next hold looked too far away. I stretched one arm as high as possible, but could not reach it. ____2____ With my foot in a better position, the same handhold was suddenly close enough.

I did not reach the top on that attempt. Our instructor helped me come down safely, then asked what had worked. ____3____ Remembering one useful movement felt better than judging the whole attempt only by its height.

Before trying again, I watched another beginner. She paused often but kept looking for her feet as well as her hands. On my second climb, I did the same. ____4____ I still needed the instructor's guidance, but I no longer thought climbing meant pulling harder with my arms alone.

A comic I could not swap

Friday, 11 October

Our class held a comic swap after lessons. Each person could bring something they owned and exchange it with a willing partner. I brought two comics from the shelf beside my bed. ____1____ I had forgotten that my cousin had only lent it to me.

At the swap, a friend chose that comic. I was about to agree when I noticed my cousin's name inside. ____2____ It was not mine to give away, even though it had been in my room for weeks.

I apologised and showed my friend the other comic. She had already read it, so we did not exchange anything. That was disappointing, but nobody said a swap was compulsory. ____3____ We talked about the ending while other pairs made their choices.

At home, I returned the borrowed comic to its separate folder and sent my cousin a message. Next time, I will check ownership before packing. ____4____ An enjoyable exchange still depends on having the right to offer what you bring.

originalGroup.material:
Finding a place for homework

A place for homework does not have to be a room used by nobody else. Many families share tables and quiet corners. Start by noticing when and how the available space is used. ____1____ A place that is empty in the afternoon may become busy when another person returns home.

Agree on a useful time

Ask rather than simply leaving your things across the whole table. You could say, "____2____" A clear request is easier to discuss than an assumption that everyone knows your plan.

Keep what you need close

Getting up repeatedly to find ordinary supplies can interrupt concentration. ____3____ A small container makes it possible to set up and clear away without moving an entire cupboard.

Separate work from distractions

Think about what usually pulls your attention away. ____4____ If you need a device for the task, keep the relevant page open rather than switching between it and unrelated messages.

____5____

After a few days, consider whether the arrangement works for you and the people sharing the space. Perhaps the agreed time clashes with dinner preparation, or the lighting is poor after dark. A small change can be more useful than insisting that the first plan must remain perfect.

Choosing a present with care

Choosing a present begins with the person receiving it, not simply with an attractive shop display. Think about what they actually enjoy and use. A hobby can suggest an idea, but it does not mean every object linked to that hobby will suit them. ____1____ The detail helps you move from a general interest to a useful choice.

Ask without spoiling everything

A small question can be better than a confident guess. You might say, "____2____" The answer can reveal a preference without requiring you to announce the exact present.

Consider practical limits

A large object may be difficult for someone with little storage space. ____3____ The thought behind a gift should include the work needed to keep or use it, not only the excitement of opening it.

Keep the choice comfortable

An expensive gift can make some people feel they must respond in the same way. ____4____ A modest present that fits the relationship may be easier to enjoy without worry.

____5____

Once you have chosen, think about how to pass it on. Remove the price label where appropriate and check whether the person will need instructions or an exchange receipt. A simple explanation of why you chose it can matter more than elaborate wrapping.

Choosing a present with care

Choosing a present begins with the person receiving it, not simply with an attractive shop display. Think about what they actually enjoy and use. A hobby can suggest an idea, but it does not mean every object linked to that hobby will suit them. ____1____ The detail helps you move from a general interest to a useful choice.

Ask without spoiling everything

A small question can be better than a confident guess. You might say, "____2____" The answer can reveal a preference without requiring you to announce the exact present.

Consider practical limits

A large object may be difficult for someone with little storage space. ____3____ The thought behind a gift should include the work needed to keep or use it, not only the excitement of opening it.

Keep the choice comfortable

An expensive gift can make some people feel they must respond in the same way. ____4____ A modest present that fits the relationship may be easier to enjoy without worry.

____5____

Once you have chosen, think about how to pass it on. Remove the price label where appropriate and check whether the person will need instructions or an exchange receipt. A simple explanation of why you chose it can matter more than elaborate wrapping.
